source.title_on_document: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence

supplement.where: Supplementary Materials referred to throughout (p. 3, Method; p. 4, Takeup; p. 5; p. 10, notes 26-27); no URL given in this PDF. Data and code on OSF (p. 11).
supplement.holds: Complete design description, survey questionnaires, objective time measures, control-group ChatGPT use, 2SLS estimates, Lee bounds, results controlling for employment and occupation, details of the 15-minute fixed-time arm, grades of raw ChatGPT output, and (presumably) the separate sub-grade results for writing quality, content quality, and originality, which the main text describes only in words.

paper_design_summary: In a preregistered online experiment on Prolific, 453 college-educated professionals (marketers, grant writers, consultants, data analysts, HR professionals, managers) each completed two occupation-specific, incentivized writing tasks; between tasks, half were randomly told to sign up for ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and allowed to use it on the second task, and the control group signed up for Overleaf. Blinded professionals from the same occupations graded each output on a 1-7 scale (overall grade plus sub-grades for writing quality, content quality, and originality), and time taken was recorded.

studies.label: Online experiment with professionals (occupation-specific writing tasks, ChatGPT vs Overleaf signup)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Instruction to register for ChatGPT between the first and second task, with guidance on using it and permission to use it on the second task (treatment), versus instruction to register for Overleaf with no permission statement (control). Bonus-payment incentive scheme was cross-randomized (linear, convex, fixed 15 minutes per task).
assignment.quote: We randomly assigned 50% of participants to the treatment group and the remainder to the control group. The treatment group was instructed to register for ChatGPT between the first and second task
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 1, Abstract; p. 11, Data and materials availability (AEA RCT Registry, trial 10882)

arms.name: Treatment (ChatGPT)
arms.description: Registered for ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) after task 1, received guidance, and were told they could use it on task 2 if useful. 92% registered and 80% used it on task 2 (p. 4).

arms.name: Control (Overleaf signup)
arms.description: Registered for the LaTeX editor Overleaf to equalize signup time and hassle; not told they could use it; less than 5% reported using it. About 10-20% of controls used ChatGPT on the tasks (p. 4).

participants.exclusions: Attrition was 6% in the control group and 11% in the treatment group (p. 3). The PDF does not print the number of people in the post-treatment grade analysis. Figure 1 restricts to the linear and convex incentive groups (80% of respondents). Table 1 arm counts (235 control, 218 treatment from the occupation rows) sum to 453; other Table 1 rows have fewer observations (e.g., task-1 grade 233 vs 211).
participants.who: Experienced, college-educated professionals recruited on Prolific: marketers, grant writers, consultants, data analysts, human resource professionals, and managers.
participants.quote: we recruited 453 experienced, college-educated professionals on the survey platform Prolific and assigned each to complete two occupation-specific, incentivized writing tasks

ai_tool.how_used: Free use of ChatGPT on the second task. Most users pasted in ChatGPT output and submitted it lightly edited or unedited: 33% reported submitting the initial output without editing, 53% reported editing, and editors were active for 3.3 minutes on average after pasting (p. 5).

task.description: Occupation-specific professional writing tasks resembling real work: press releases, short reports, analysis plans, and delicate emails. Two tasks per person; task 1 without AI (baseline), task 2 after assignment.
task.duration: 20- to 30-minute assignments; in the fixed-time incentive arm (20% of participants), exactly 15 minutes per task

outcomes.name: Average evaluator grade on the post-treatment task (1-7 scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Blinded experienced professionals in the same occupations graded each output on 1-7, treating it as encountered at work; three evaluators per output; average cross-evaluator correlation 0.44; evaluators incentivized by agreement with other evaluators (p. 3; p. 9, note 22). Effect in SDs of the pre-treatment outcome, from a participant-evaluator level regression of the pre-to-post change on treatment with occupation*task-order, incentive-arm, and grader fixed effects; SEs clustered by person (p. 12, Fig. 1 note).

contrasts.reported: Text (all incentive arms implied): 'Average evaluator grades in the treatment group increased by 0.45 standard deviations (p<0.001)'. Fig. 1B (linear and convex arms only): Treatment Effect 0.41 SDs, 95% CI [0.23, 0.59]. Fig. 1D second-task grade means (essay-grade level): Control 3.802, Treatment 4.53. Abstract: output quality rose by 18%.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Productivity, lines 18-20; p. 12, Fig. 1 panels B and D; p. 1, Abstract

contrasts.reported: 'the treatment increased grades by a similar albeit not statistically significant 0.33 standard deviations'; note 26: confidence interval includes zero and arms differ in pre-treatment grades. Subgroup is 20% of participants.

company_involvement.description: Funding from Emergent Ventures (Mercatus Center), MIT Economics Department, and an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship; authors declare no competing interests. No AI company involvement stated.

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to ChatGPT access versus an Overleaf-signup control (p. 3). 453 people were assigned; attrition was 6% and 11%, so the analyzed count is far above 50, although the PDF does not print it. Outputs were graded by blinded professionals, including an originality sub-grade (p. 4). Borderline on scope: the tasks are professional writing (press releases, reports, analysis plans, emails) judged mainly on quality; creativity enters only as an originality sub-grade whose estimate sits in the Supplementary Materials, not in this PDF.

one_line_finding: Random access to ChatGPT raised blinded professional graders' average grades on professional writing tasks by 0.45 SD (p<0.001; Fig. 1B, linear and convex arms: 0.41 SD, 95% CI [0.23, 0.59]), with 'similar increases' for the originality sub-grade stated without numbers (p. 4; p. 12).
open_questions: Does occupational writing (press releases, reports, analysis plans, delicate emails) graded mainly on quality fall within the creativity section's scope, given that only the originality sub-grade is a creativity construct?
The originality sub-grade estimate and its SE are not printed in this PDF; extraction needs the Science Supplementary Materials or the OSF data.
Text reports 0.45 SD for average grades while Fig. 1B reports 0.41 SD for the linear and convex arms only; which sample the 0.45 refers to is not stated explicitly.
The number of people in the post-treatment grade analysis is not printed; Table 1 arm counts (235/218) appear to be the assigned sample.
notes: Time taken (-0.75 SD, Fig. 1A), productivity inequality (Fig. 2), job satisfaction, self-efficacy, automation beliefs (Fig. 3), and follow-up ChatGPT use are not creativity outcomes and are not listed. Contamination: about 10-20% of controls used ChatGPT, so estimates are intention-to-treat style lower bounds per the authors; 2SLS is in the supplement. A side intervention let 30% of the treatment group edit or replace their task-1 output with ChatGPT (p. 4); no grades reported for it. Arm n_randomized (235, 218) taken from Table 1 occupation rows, which sum to the 453 recruited; the paper does not label them as counts at assignment. Per retrieval.json, the earlier MIT working paper (March 10, 2023) is a different draft with 444 participants; not used here.
